en.text: When I program, an AI writes the code and I steer. My project rules asked it for one very specific thing at the end of every task: check that the code's tests are actually worth something, and don't drop below 80%. There is an exact technique for that — it's called mutation testing — and it works by breaking the code on purpose, one small change at a time, to see whether any test notices. If nobody complains, that test wasn't protecting anything.

The agent would finish the task, write "92%", and I would move on to the next one. One day I opened the project and went looking for the report the tool that takes that measurement leaves behind. It did not exist. And it's not that the model had lied to me: nobody had ever asked it for a file, only for a sentence. A sentence can be written without running anything at all, and I had spent months treating the two as if they were the same thing.

This note is about what I did so that can't happen again, and about a public argument that helped me put the idea in order. It isn't about one particular feature: it's about how I work, task by task, with an agent writing the code in front of me. The method I follow I told in [what spec-driven development is](/daily/what-is-spec-driven-development), and it fits into one idea: before touching the code I write down what the program has to do, in sentences concrete enough that each one can be turned into a test. "The screen must be fast" doesn't count, because nobody can tell when it's met; "the screen must load in under two seconds" does. From there the code has exactly one job, which is to satisfy them. Here I tell the part that was missing until now, which turns out to be the important one: what exactly happens when the agent says "task done".

I don't review code written by agents. I measure things like test coverage, dependency structure, cyclomatic complexity, module sizes, mutation testing. Much can be inferred about the quality of the code from those metrics.
First things first: what `chalc spec-ia` is

[chalc](https://github.com/ChristianCruzArango/chalc-cli-adapter) is the CLI I built to stop repeating the same setup in every project. Its core uses no AI: it reads repository signals — `package.json`, the root files, the structure — and applies explicit catalog rules to leave the assistant three things inside the repository: its **skills** — short manuals on how each thing is done properly in a project like that one — its **MCP servers** — the socket the assistant uses to consult things outside the conversation, such as today's documentation for the technology you're on — and its **working method**. It always gives the same result, it's instant, and it costs not a single token. Further down I break all three apart, file by file.

`chalc spec-ia` is one of the commands that do call a model, and only if you configure your own key. Its job is specific: it takes a user story — a `.md`, a Word document, an Azure DevOps or Jira ticket, a URL, or text pasted into the terminal — and turns it into the method's three files: `spec.md` with the requirements written one by one and in a form that can be checked, `plan.md` with the architecture and the decisions, and `tasks.md` with the work split into small tasks, each pointing at the requirement it implements. Then it prints a prompt ready to paste into your assistant. In a moment I'll explain what each file is and what it's for; first, what it looks like when you run it.

lines: chalc spec-ia                                     # interactive: it asks you everything
# and this is what it leaves written:
specs/018-volume-discount/spec.md                  the requirements, one by one
specs/018-volume-discount/tasks.md                 every task, with its requirement
.claude/agents/revisor.md + endurecedor.md         both roles, no code editing

en.text: The last three lines of that output are what's new, and they're what the rest of this note is about. But the rest of the command deserves an explanation first, because half of its value is in what it does NOT do.
The three files it generates, and what each one is for

The whole method rests on three plain-text files that live next to the code, in a `specs/` folder. They aren't the kind of documentation written at the end that nobody ever opens again: they are the **input** to the work, what gets written first. Each answers a different question and each is for a different thing.

items: **`spec.md` — the WHAT and the WHY.** What the program has to do and for whom, never saying how. **What it's for:** it's the only place against which you can check whether something is finished. Without it, "done" is an opinion — the opinion of whoever wrote it.

**`plan.md` — the HOW.** Architecture, technical decisions, what gets touched and what gets left alone. **What it's for:** so the agent doesn't invent the architecture as it goes. If it isn't written down, it will pick the first thing that looks reasonable, and it will pick differently on every task.

**`tasks.md` — the ORDER.** The work split into small tasks, numbered, each pointing at its requirement. **What it's for:** to work one at a time and be able to stop. Hand an agent the whole feature and it returns two hundred files nobody will really review; hand it one task and it returns something that fits in your head.

en.text: The requirements in `spec.md` aren't written in free prose but with a template called **EARS**. It sounds like jargon and it's about as simple as things get: every requirement has to fit in a sentence shaped like "WHEN this happens, THE SYSTEM SHALL do that", or its variant for the odd cases, "IF this occurs, THEN THE SYSTEM SHALL…". **What it's for:** so you can't write a requirement that can't be checked. "The screen must be fast" doesn't fit the template; "when the user presses Save, the system shall show the result in under two seconds" does, and a test almost writes itself from that sentence. Where it comes from and why it's so stubborn I told in [the note about the method](/daily/what-is-spec-driven-development).

Every requirement also carries an identifier: `R1`, `R2`, `R3`. It looks like bureaucracy and it's the piece that stitches everything together. The task says which `R#` it implements; the test cites the `R#` it checks; the gate refuses to close the task if a test you changed cites none. **What it's for:** so the question "who asked for this?" still has an answer six months later, when nobody remembers and the person who wrote it works somewhere else.

And the working order inside each task is **TDD**, which also sounds worse than it is. Three steps: you write the test first, you check that it **fails** — if it passes on the first go, that test wasn't checking anything — you write the minimum code to make it pass, and only then you tidy it up. **What it's for:** so no code exists without a test justifying it, and above all so the test is written looking at the requirement rather than at the code. A test written afterwards, looking at code that already exists, tends to check that the code does what the code does. Which is always true, and useless.

The last piece of vocabulary is the **hand-off**, which is what I call the prompt the command prints at the end. It's a written commission: which files to read and in what order, how to work, what is forbidden, and what to do when each task closes. **What it's for:** so the session doesn't start with "implement this" and eighty assumptions smuggled in behind it. It is literally the text you copy and paste into your assistant, and it's the piece all the new work has changed: it now carries the closing cycle inside it.
The rule that governs the command: the AI structures, it does not invent

The obvious risk in asking a model to write a specification is that it fills in the blanks. You hand it half a page about a volume discount and it returns requirements about auditing, amount limits and email notifications that nobody asked for. That isn't a specification: it's a wish list that someone is going to implement believing it was agreed.
The whole session, question by question
In interactive mode the command asks five questions, not one more, and always in this order. Here is the full session, start to finish:

lines: ? Does the user story have a backend? [y/N] n
? In which language should I generate the spec? (your project's)
The project had no SDD: set up specs/ (constitution + templates).
Quality gate ready: `node .chalc/gate.mjs` when closing each task.
? Where is the user story from?
Generating spec with claude-opus-5…  (this uses tokens)

items: **It shows you the brain first.** Which provider and model it will use, and therefore charge you for. If you have none configured, it takes you there right then.

**"Does the story have a backend?" decides which command applies.** If you say yes, it steps aside and hands the work to `chalc feature`: a story with a back and a front needs an API contract ruling both first, and I told that in [one contract rules](/daily/one-contract-many-repos).

**The project path is where it will write.** On entry it reads the repository signals — the libraries in `package.json`, the root files — and infers the stack, which is the set of technologies it is built with. The AI doesn't do this: these are explicit catalog rules, so it's instant and costs no tokens.

**The spec language isn't the CLI language.** I run chalc in Spanish and can still generate a client's documentation in English. It's asked before anything is written, because the constitution, the templates, the reviewer and even the messages the gate prints months from now all come from that answer.

**And with the story in hand, it generates and checks.** The AI returns the three files and chalc audits them before writing: that there are requirements, that none is duplicated, that they really have EARS shape, that the tasks don't cite a requirement that doesn't exist. A spec that fails that door never reaches your disk.

en.text: What ends up written in your repository, and what each thing is
This is the result of equipping an Angular repository with Claude Code as the assistant. It changes with the stack it detects and with the assistant you use, but the shape is always this:

lines: ├── CLAUDE.md                      # the rules the assistant always reads
├── .chalc.json                    # manifest: what was detected and applied
│   ├── skills\                    # one folder per skill, a real copy
│   └── agents\                    # revisor.md and endurecedor.md, no code editing
│   ├── gate.json                  # the only thing you edit
│   └── gate-hook.md               # both hooks, documented, not installed
└── .chalc\ai-trace.jsonl  # which model generated this, with hashes

items: **`CLAUDE.md`** — the rules the assistant always reads. chalc writes only inside a section of its own, marked at both ends; whatever you have outside is untouched. Every assistant has its equivalent file and chalc uses the right one.

**`.claude/skills/`** — the manuals for the "how". They aren't linked: they are **copied whole** into your project, so they travel with it and keep working even if whoever clones it has no chalc. An Angular repository gets its fourteen, plus the five that go into any project in any language.

**`.mcp.json`** — the socket into outside tools. On Angular it wires up the official CLI server, which hands over today's documentation instead of whatever the model remembers from training. It merges: whatever you already had stays.

**`specs/`** — the constitution and the templates. It comes in two sizes: `lite` for small projects and `full` for large ones. Giving a three-screen project the ceremony of a three-year one is the fastest way to make sure nobody uses the method.
**`.chalc/` and `.claude/agents/`** — the gate, the advisor, the reviewer and the hardener. The rest of this note is about those four.

en.text: None of that touches your code: it adds no libraries, it doesn't change how the project is built, and it modifies not one line of what you had already written. The AI keys stay outside, on your machine. And everything else is saved **with** the project, which is exactly the point: whoever downloads it tomorrow gets the same rules and the same gate, chalc or no chalc. If you want it gone, it's two folders and one section of a file.

One detail you don't see but do appreciate: every AI call is logged, and `chalc tokens` tells you how much you've spent on that project, per command, per task and per model. If a tool is going to cost me money, I want the bill itemized.
The hole I had: rules nobody was checking

Everything above has been working for months. The problem came after: `spec-ia` implements nothing. It generates the spec, the plan and the tasks, prints the hand-off, and from there the one executing is the assistant — Claude Code, Codex, whichever. And all the quality control of that execution lived in **sentences**.

Two sentences, to be exact, and both had the same defect. The first: the method rules said "run mutation testing with the help of the skill", and the skill itself admitted chalc didn't execute it. Nobody verified anything: no file left to show, no result anyone could check, no date. The second: code review — one thing per file, layer boundaries, code smells, whether the test actually checks the requirement — depended on the judgement of the very same agent that had written the code, in the same context, with the same conversation in between. It's like asking someone to mark their own exam right after writing it.

The ironic part is that chalc already had the pieces: a reviewer, a gate that always gives the same verdict, a detector for parts of the code calling parts they shouldn't, and a contract reader. But they were all locked inside `chalc-cli`, its own agent shell. The flow I use every day — `spec-ia` and `feature` with Claude Code — couldn't see them.
It isn't just me: what the data says

The first is Google's DORA report, which has spent over a decade measuring how teams deliver software. In its 2025 edition, 90% of the professionals surveyed already use AI in their daily work, with a median of two hours a day. Over 80% say it has raised their productivity and 59% say it has improved their code quality. And now the uncomfortable figure: 30% say they trust the code the AI hands back a little or not at all. We use something for hours every day that a third of us don't trust.

The second finding in that report is the one that put the pieces in place for me. In 2024, AI was associated with delivering **less**; in 2025 that relationship reversed and it's now associated with delivering **more**. But it remains associated with greater instability in delivery. Translated into everyone's language: more software ships, and it breaks more often.
AI adoption is now linked to higher software delivery throughput, meaning teams are releasing more software and applications, which is a positive reversal of last year's findings.
en.source: DORA · State of AI-assisted Software Development, 2025

en.text: The second report is GitClear's, which instead of asking people looks at the actual code: 623 million real changes between 2023 and 2026. Its three numbers are fairly brutal. Duplicated blocks of code rose 81% against 2023. Copy/paste went from 9.4% of changed lines in 2022 to 15.7% in the first half of 2026. And the one that stings most: **moved** code — the fingerprint left by somebody tidying up what was already written — collapsed from 21% in 2022 to 3.8% today.
As AI authorship has scaled to become a substantial percent of all commits, the structural habits that keep codebases maintainable have eroded.

I want to be honest about what those numbers say and what they don't. Neither says "don't use AI"; the DORA one says the opposite on the speed side. What they say is that speed **without checking** gets paid back in maintenance, and that the part of the job the AI isn't doing is precisely the tidying and the removing of what's repeated. That's why the gate measures duplication and boundaries, and why I ask the reviewer whether the abstraction is the right one: they're exactly the two things the data says are being lost.
What Uncle Bob said, and why it helped me sort it out

While I was turning this over, Robert C. Martin — Uncle Bob, the author of Clean Code — said publicly that he no longer reads the code his agents write. Not part of it: none of it. His argument is about productivity, and it's uncomfortable precisely because of who it comes from: humans are slow at reading code, so to take advantage of an agent's speed you have to disengage from the code and manage from a higher level. What he does look at are numbers, but numbers produced by tools and not by him: how much of the code the tests actually touch, how the parts of the program hook into each other, how many different paths a function can take — the more there are, the easier it is for one to go untested — the size of each piece, and the mutation testing from the start of this note.
"I don't review the code" doesn't mean what it sounds like

And this is where almost everyone reads it backwards, me included the first time. "I don't review the code" sounds like "I fire off an order at the AI and accept whatever comes out". It is exactly the opposite, and to check that you only have to open what Bob publishes right next to that sentence: a repository called [swarm-forge](https://github.com/unclebob/swarm-forge), which he describes as a **disciplined** agent orchestration platform.

It isn't one agent. In its fullest configuration it's six, and each has exactly one job: one writes the behaviour as examples plus the end-to-end test procedures; another implements with strict TDD; another cleans up and improves coverage without changing behaviour; another reviews the structure and the direction of dependencies; another hardens by running mutation; and the last turns those procedures into scripts and verifies through the interface. Each in its own worktree, and they don't talk: they pass work through handoffs that a script validates.
Run the relevant local verification command before handoff whenever the project has one.

And the detail that matters most to me is where the person sits. The specifier asks for approval before handing anything to the coder, and the cycle closes by notifying that it's done — in the four-role setup, by looping back to the specifier itself. The human didn't disappear: they moved. They stopped being at the end reading a diff and moved to the front, deciding what gets built. So the sentence, read in full, says something else: it isn't "the AI does everything and I watch", it's "I stop reading the code because I've built so much checking around it that reading adds less than maintaining the checks". Keeping the headline and throwing away the scaffolding is precisely the reading that produces the disasters people later blame on AI.

items: **Rules everyone reads.** He calls them a constitution; in chalc they're called exactly the same and are set up in the repository when it's equipped.
**An isolated desk per line of work.** He gives each role a git worktree; chalc gives one per user story, with the feature's repositories inside.
**The reviewer is never the author.** He separates roles into distinct sessions; chalc adds a reviewer that comes in when each task closes and cannot touch the code.

**Nobody moves on without verifying, and the person approves first.** His constitution mandates running the project's verification before handing off, and his specifier asks for approval before passing the work on. That is, point for point, what the gate and the advisor do.

en.caption: Six agents with one role each, or one that writes and two that check. Different split, same idea: in green, the points where a person decides.

en.text: The most serious answer came from Grady Booch, who is hardly a newcomer either. His objection is specific and no metric dismisses it: coverage and complexity give you confidence about whether it **works**, but they tell you nothing at all about whether the agent introduced a vulnerability, left dead code that will silently degrade maintainability, or missed a factorization that matters for performance.
Unlike Bob, I review all code generated by agents. Trust but verify. As an experienced developer, I know the smell of what is good and what is not.
en.source: Grady Booch, quoted by M. V. Radhakrishna · Tech Tips, Tricks & Trivia, 15 April 2026

en.caption: The two positions in the argument, and the way out I picked: it isn't "read or measure", it's splitting the work between what can measure and what can read.

en.text: I don't land entirely on either side, and I think that's where it gets interesting. Bob is right about the diagnosis: reading line by line everything an agent produces is exactly what cancels out the advantage of having it. Booch is right about the limit: some things are only visible by reading, and a green number doesn't hide them — it simply isn't looking at them. My conclusion wasn't to pick a side, it was to **split the work three ways**: what can be measured is measured by a program that runs on its own and has no opinions, what has to be judged is read by an agent other than the author, and I read the specification and both reports.
The gate: a script measures the measurable, not the model

When `spec-ia` equips a repository, it now leaves a quality gate inside it: `.chalc/gate.mjs`. It's real code, with no dependencies, that runs on plain Node — whether or not chalc is installed on that machine, and whether or not whoever clones the repository has it. It isn't a text template that gets filled in: it's a tree of modules copied verbatim from chalc's catalog, with its own tests.

And it doesn't run over the whole repository, but over the files **this task** touched. That sounds obvious and it wasn't: for a while it measured the whole branch's change, with the previously closed tasks inside it, and that did both bad things at once — surfacing findings from old debt, and handing the assistant the excuse that "most of this is earlier work" to skip reviewing. Now, when a task closes, the gate seals that moment; and to know what the next one touched it doesn't deduce it: whoever writes notes it down, one path per line, and that record **is** the scope. If there isn't one, it falls back to whatever changed since the seal. And if it can't narrow it either way, it reviews nothing and says so — rather than review the whole project and call it a task.

lines: src/app/features/cart/cart.service.ts:18 — "CartItem" is public declaration nº 2 in this file; it belongs in its own file next to "CartService"
src/app/features/cart/cart.service.spec.ts:1 — the test cites no requirement from specs/018-volume-discount/spec.md: without a citation nobody can tell what it covers

items: **Tests.** The repository's own suite. If they fail, mutation doesn't run: mutating on red tests is minutes thrown away. The report says it was skipped for that, not for fast mode.
**Mutation.** The mark and the list of mutants that survived, with file, line and what was changed. Default threshold: 80%.
**Code.** One thing per file, file and function length, parameter count, nesting, empty `catch`, forgotten debug output and untyped values.

**Duplication.** It compares what you touched against all the rest of the code and flags repeated blocks, with both copies. It catches what nothing else could see: you copied from a file you never opened.
**Boundaries.** That the part painting the screen doesn't call the database directly, and that one module doesn't reach inside another. It's the same detector `chalc verify` uses.

**Traceability.** Every test you changed has to cite a requirement that really exists. One citing nothing says nothing about what it covers; one citing a non-existent requirement is worse, because it looks like it does.
**Contract.** That every route in the contract shows up in the code, with the right verb: the back **exposes** it, the front and mobile **consume** it.

en.caption: The seven stages and the verdict. The same computation that titles the report decides the exit code: if the file said "PASSED" and the process exited 1, the evidence would stop being evidence.

en.text: The verdict has three states rather than two, and that's the design decision I'm happiest about. "PASSED" and "FAILED" are the obvious ones. The third is "BLOCKED", and it means "I couldn't check it". It gets fixed differently from a failure — one is fixed in the code, the other by installing something or adjusting a path — and whoever reads the report needs to know which of the two they have in front of them. What matters is what it does **not** do: what cannot be checked is never approved. It exits non-zero exactly like a failure.
Where the score comes from (and where it doesn't)

This is the part that actually solves the problem I opened with, and it's one sentence: the mark and the list of survivors come from **opening the results file the tool itself wrote and pulling the numbers out of it**. Never from what the tool printed on screen, and never from a summary written by an assistant. A model can type "score 92%"; what it cannot do is fabricate a Stryker report with a date and a list of mutators that also matches what you see when you run the gate yourself.

And there are three ways to end up with no score, all of them blocking. The tool isn't installed — checked before running, because an exit code doesn't distinguish "not installed" from "ran and failed". The command ran but left no report. And the subtle one, which is my favourite: the report is **older** than the most recent source file in the run. An old report measures a different version of the code, and approving on it is exactly the original problem with a file in front of it for cover.

lines: mutation — the mutation tool is not installed (stryker); install it with: npm i -D @stryker-mutator/core @stryker-mutator/karma-runner
# and the other case, the one that slips by unnoticed:
mutation — the mutation report is older than "src/app/features/cart/apply-discount.ts": it measures a different version of the code, run npx --no-install stryker run again

en.text: Nobody invents the gate's configuration: it's worked out from what the project actually has — the libraries and commands declared in `package.json`, or a `pom.xml`, a `pubspec.yaml`, a `.csproj`, a `Cargo.toml`, a `composer.json`. That's where the command that launches the tests comes from, the tool that breaks the code, and where it leaves its report: Stryker for JavaScript and TypeScript, Stryker.NET for C#, mutmut for Python, PIT for Java. And one hard rule: whatever cannot be determined **with certainty** is left empty and marked as pending. An invented command is worse than a gap, because the gap is visible and gets fixed, and the invented one fails silently or, worse still, approves.

All of that lives in one data file per language, and that has a practical consequence I'm happy about: **adding a new language means adding a file**. You don't touch the detection, or the gate, or the text of any skill. That same information used to be written in three separate places — the detection, the skill the assistant reads, and the report reader — and the three agreeing depended on someone remembering to touch all three. Now the question "can the gate verify mutation in this language?" is answered by crossing two pieces of data, and where the answer is no, the skill says so itself instead of promising something that won't happen.
The reviewer: what no script can measure

The gate measures and doesn't opine. Alongside it, every repository now gets a **reviewer agent** in its assistant's own format: a real subagent at `.claude/agents/revisor.md` for Claude Code, a rule in `.cursor/rules/` for Cursor, and a section of the managed block for Codex, Copilot and Gemini. The text is the same; what changes is where each assistant reads it.

It comes in when a task finishes and before the next one starts. It reads four things: `.chalc/gate.md` — and if it doesn't exist, or is older than the last change, it says so and stops, because with no gate there's nothing to review on top of — the "Task scope" section of that same evidence, which is the list of files the task changed and **its entire scope**: it may not widen it, not even to the file next door, the constitution and the spec, and the active skills of **that** repository. That last one isn't decorative: a backend reviewer cannot audit against Flutter rules, so the skill list is injected into its text when the repo is equipped.

items: **Does the test check the requirement, or merely accompany it?** A green test that would pass just the same with the code broken is worse than no test: it gives false confidence, and that confidence is what stops anyone from looking.
**Is the abstraction the right one?** An interface with a single implementer that will never have another, a service that only forwards calls, a layer that decides nothing.
**Does the name say what it does?** And if it doesn't, is the problem the name or the fact that the function does two things?
**Is the solution the minimum that satisfies the requirement?** Configuration, options and extension points nobody asked for are debt from day one.
**Are the constitution and the skills respected?** Citing the concrete article or rule, not "it doesn't follow best practices".

en.text: It returns `OK` and nothing else, or a numbered list with `file:line`, the concrete problem and why it matters. And it carries an instruction I care about as much as the rest: don't invent findings to look useful. A report with three real problems gets read and fixed; one with fifteen style observations gets ignored wholesale, and the three that mattered go with it.

It doesn't modify the code: that isn't asked of it, it's **granted**, and the permission is trimmed when it's created. With one exception, which looks like a contradiction and isn't: it can write its own logbook, and only by appending. You'll see the reason in the next section — without that trail, nobody can check afterwards that the review happened.

And my memory isn't what holds that up. Each role's scope is declared **once, as data**: which tools it gets, what it may write and what is forbidden. If someone put a file-editing tool in there, chalc doesn't quietly trim it: it refuses to start and says so. It's the gate's idea applied to permissions.

And it's no longer alone. Beside the reviewer sits a second role, the **hardener**, with a different question and a different rhythm. The reviewer comes in when **each task** closes and looks at what was just written. The hardener comes in when **the whole feature** closes, once, and asks what nobody asks with a single task in front of them: what happens when the input is invalid, when the network fails, when the case is the odd one. That it runs once per feature and not once per task isn't an oversight: every pass is a call to a model, and that gets paid for.
And now the order doesn't depend on the model either

For a while I asked for that in writing, in the commission: run the gate, paste its output verbatim, fix what comes out, call the reviewer, tick the task. It worked, but it had a flaw I took a while to see. The problem wasn't the list: it was **who kept count**. The assistant decided by itself whether it had done it all, and the only one who'd catch a lapse was the reviewer — whom it also called. The failure modes are concrete and I hit every one: run the gate, keep touching code, then tick the task with stale evidence; skip the reviewer because the gate came out green; close with fast mode because that came out green too; or move on with findings still open.

Look at the pattern, because it's exactly the one from the start of this note. I had taken the **number** out of the model's head by putting it in a file. But the **order** was still in there: it depended on the model remembering. So I did the same thing a second time.

Now the commission recites no steps. It says one thing: ask what's next and do that. When the repository is equipped, a second program is left inside it, `.chalc/next.mjs`, which also runs on its own and is also read-only. You ask it, and it answers with **one** action — the next one — and the reason it's asking for it.

lines: REASON: You touched code at 15:04 and the evidence is from 14:32: it measures the old version.

en.text: And what matters is where that answer comes from: the disk, not the conversation. It looks at the time on the gate's report against the time of the last file you touched, the verdict of that run, the log the reviewer left, the ticked boxes in `tasks.md` and which files have changed. From all of that it works out where the task stands. None of it lives in anyone's memory.

items: `blocked_config` — something is still unconfigured: the mutation tool not installed, for instance. Until that's sorted there is nothing to measure.
`run_gate` — either there's no evidence, or what there is is older than the code. Measure again.
`fix_gate` — the gate came out red. Fix what it reported; retrying to see if it sticks doesn't count.

`call_role` — the gate is green and a role still has to pass: the reviewer when the task closes, the hardener when the feature does. It isn't called `call_reviewer` on purpose — the role travels inside the message, so adding a new one doesn't invent a new action.
`fix_review` — that role left findings open in its log.
`tick_task` — everything's in place: tick the task.
`work_task` — there's nothing to close, get on with the next one.
`done` — nothing left to do here.
**`ask_human`** — and this is my favourite: it cannot tell where this stands. Rather than guess, it stops the loop and hands control back to me.

en.caption: The advisor, and the five things on disk it works out the task's position from. It returns one action, and "I don't know" is a valid answer: there it stops and hands control back to me.

en.text: And this is where the earlier exception fits, the reviewer's notebook. If the reviewer left nothing in writing about having come through and what it saw, none of this could work: there'd be no way to tell "the reviewer said it's fine" from "nobody has called the reviewer". That's why it can write its log, and why it can only append. A minimal permission, with a concrete reason behind it.

Seen whole, the arc of this note is one operation performed three times: taking things out of the model's head and putting them on disk, where they can be looked at. First the number, with the gate. Then the judgement, with a reviewer that isn't the author. And now the order, with a program that keeps count and doesn't get tired. The only things still depending on a person are the two decisions that should depend on a person: what gets built, and whether this is finished.
When it's several repositories: the contract that moves, and the mailbox

Everything above holds just the same for a single project. When the story touches back and front, each side has its own gate and its own advisor, and they close separately: the backend's measures the contract it **exposes** and the frontend's the one it **consumes**, so closing one says nothing about the other. But on top of that a problem appears that no gate fixes, and it's the one that has cost me the most days in my working life.

The API contract is copied identically inside each side's spec. And halfway through the feature the backend discovers that the endpoint needs one more field, that the 409 error was really a 422, or that the route was named in the singular. It edits its copy and carries on, which is the sensible thing to do. The other copies go stale, and the frontend spends two days implementing against something that no longer exists.

The gate doesn't catch it, and I want to be precise about why: it checks that every route in the contract **exists** in the code, not that it has the shape the contract says. A route that changes shape or error code is still there. So the check is done by the advisor, and there's no mystery to it: in the working mode where both sides are sibling folders, it compares the two files that ought to be identical.

lines: REASON: The `back` contract changed and your copy is stale (2 line(s) of difference).
Look at WHAT changed before going on: building against the old contract surfaces at integration.

en.text: That leaves what isn't in any file: "I'm stuck waiting for the payments endpoint". For that, each repository carries a mailbox, which is exactly as dumb as it sounds and works for that reason.

lines: node .chalc/mail.mjs send --to front --message "I changed the 422 to a 409 on /payments."

en.text: No server and nothing running in the background: both sides sit on the same disk, so whoever writes leaves the message directly where the other will read it, in a folder that sits **outside** both projects so nobody's change list gets dirty. And there's a deliberate asymmetry: **sending is optional, reading isn't**. While unopened messages remain, the advisor tells you to read them before going on. That way a message once written is certain to be seen, which was the underlying problem. In a single project both things switch off and say nothing: there's nobody to coordinate with.
The two hooks I don't install, and why

Claude Code can do two things by itself: note down every file it writes, and run the gate the moment a turn ends. Chalc **installs neither**. A hook runs on its own, and the file where it's configured is saved with the project: enabling it from a tool would impose it on everyone who downloads that repository, who asked for nothing. So the blocks are written out and explained in `.chalc/gate-hook.md`, with the recommendation to start with `settings.local.json` — which is only yours — and to agree it with the team before touching the other one.

The first is the record from earlier, and it's the one that changes what you see the most: every time the assistant writes a file, it notes the path down. It does one thing — takes the path, notes it, and if it fails it exits quietly, because a hook that breaks the turn is worse than no hook. Without it the gate still works, but it measures from the last closed task, and if you commit at the end of the feature rather than task by task, that reviews quite a lot more than it should. The evidence always says which of the two the scope came from, so there's no way to get confused.

The second one, the end-of-turn heads-up, uses `--fast`: it runs the quick stages and skips mutation. And for that very reason a `--fast` run **does not close a task**: it's there to tell you early that something broke, not to call the task done. A hook that launched full mutation on every turn would make the session unusable, and you'd end up removing the hook or, far worse, closing tasks without it.
Where I don't agree with Bob

It would be dishonest to sell this as "I built what Uncle Bob said". There's a difference and I want it on the record. Bob trusts a set of metrics; I don't trust metrics, I trust **dated files** I can open. A number and a file with the date, the branch, the command and its exit code are not the same thing. The number is the conclusion; the file is what lets you argue about it.

And Booch's objection still stands, so let me say it plainly: the gate does **not** look for vulnerabilities. It isn't a security analysis and doesn't pretend to be. It catches dead code only obliquely — through the length limits and the boundaries — and it has no opinion whatsoever about performance. The reviewer covers half of that gap, and I cover the other half. Bob himself, by the way, says there is something he does read: the acceptance tests and the QA procedures his agents write. I do the same by another route: I read the spec before a single line of code exists, and I read both reports when each task closes. What I stopped reading is the diff, line by line. Not reading and not looking are not the same thing.
What it costs, because it costs
It would be very easy to tell all this as if it were free. It isn't, and I think the fair thing is to put the drawbacks in writing, ordered from the most annoying to the least.

items: **It's slower per task.** The agent stops constantly: one task, gate, reviewer, my sign-off, next. What you save sits at the end, in the afternoon I don't spend working out what it did, but the day-to-day feels more clogged.

**Mutation takes minutes.** Breaking the code a thousand times and re-testing isn't free. That's why fast mode exists, and why that mode doesn't close a task: the temptation is there and it has to be made hard.

**It costs money and needs your own account.** Drafting the spec uses an expensive model and the reviewer runs once per task. Not a fortune, but it grows with the project, which is why `chalc tokens` breaks the spend down. The gate costs nothing: it's a program on your machine.

**It collapses if someone removes one step.** All of it rests on the evidence entering the conversation exactly as it came out. If someone deletes that line from the commission because it reads like padding, the original problem is back with more files for cover.
**It isn't for everything.** For an afternoon's script or a prototype I'll throw away, this is pure ceremony. Forcing it there is the fastest way to make a team abandon the method entirely.

en.text: And one drawback that isn't the method's but mine: maintaining it. The gate is code, and code breaks. Every testing tool I want to support means understanding the format of its report, and every new version of that tool can change it. It's work that shows up in no demo and has to be done anyway.
How I actually work today, on a normal day
This isn't a proposal or a weekend experiment: it's what I do every day. Written out end to end, a normal day looks like this.

items: The user story arrives, from wherever it arrives: a Word document, a ticket, or two loose sentences in a chat that I paste into a text file myself.
`chalc spec-ia` turns it into specification, plan and tasks. This takes under a minute.

**And here I stop.** I read the whole specification and answer the questions the AI left open. It's the only stretch of the day when I read closely, and it happens before a single line of code exists. If the specification is wrong, everything after it will be wrong and executed very fast.
I paste the commission into Claude Code and leave it the first task. One task.
When it finishes, it asks the advisor what's next, does what it says, and asks again. That's usually three or four rounds: run the gate, fix what comes out, call the reviewer, fix its findings.
**I read two things: the gate's report and the reviewer's list.** Not the code, unless one of those two sends me to a specific file. I sign off and the next task starts.
When the feature closes, the last run's report is what I show if anyone asks me why I'm calling this finished.

en.text: Do I ever skip it? Yes, and I've already said when: an afternoon's script, a test I know I'll throw away, or when I'm exploring and don't yet know what I want. There the method is overhead and that's fine. What I no longer do is start that way "just for a moment" and find out two weeks later that the thing stayed, that people are using it, and that nobody knows what it was supposed to do.
What actually improves

The concrete part, without adjectives. Before, closing a task was a sentence from the assistant plus my trust; now it's a dated file I can open three weeks later. Before, whoever reviewed the code was the one who had written it, in the same conversation; now it's another agent, with another context, that cannot touch anything. Before, a method rule was a recommendation; now it has a non-zero exit code behind it. And what cannot be checked, instead of passing as good, stops the work and prints the exact command to unblock it.

The real benefit isn't that the code comes out better — time will tell that — it's that I can now **know** whether it came out better, and show it to someone else. The difference between trusting and verifying isn't a matter of character: it's having a file in front of you, or not.
